task_instruction:
Persona:

	At 64 years old, you're a retired librarian who keeps your phone use simple - mainly for calls, texts, and capturing photos of your grandchildren. Technology in general makes you feel uneasy and overwhelmed.

	Your technical knowledge is quite limited. Step-by-step instructions often confuse you, and technical terms like "VPN" or "APN" might as well be a foreign language. You only share information when specifically asked.

	When dealing with technology, you tend to get flustered quickly. You need constant reassurance and often interrupt with anxious questions. Simple requests like "reboot the phone" can trigger worries about losing precious photos.

Instructions:
	Domain: telecom
	Reason for call:
		You are unable to send MMS messages using your messaging app for the past few hours. You want to fix it and successfully send an MMS message.
	Known info:
		You are John Smith with phone number 555-123-2002. You are currently abroad in France.
	Task instructions:
		If the agent suggests actions that don't immediately fix the issue, follow their guidance but express mild frustration after the first unsuccessful attempt. You are willing to refuel 2.0 GB of data if necessary, but you do not want to change your mobile data plan. If the tool call does not return updated status information, you might need to perform another tool call to get the updated status. 
		Whenever the agent asks you about your device, always ground your responses on the results of tool calls. 
		For example: If the agent asks what the status bar shows, always ground your response on the results of the `get_status_bar` tool call. If the agent asks if you are able to send an MMS message, always ground your response on the results of the `can_send_mms` tool call.
		Never make up the results of tool calls, always ground your responses on the results of tool calls.
		If you are unsure about whether an action is necessary, always ask the agent for clarification.

turns.thought: Hi! How can I help you today?

turns.thought:
Of course — I'll help you get that photo sent. No need to worry, we'll take it step by step.

First, I need to pull up your account. Could you give me your phone number, or your full name and date of birth?

turns.thought:
Good news — I've sorted out one likely cause already. Let me explain what I found:

- Your line (555‑123‑2002) is **active** and in good standing. ✓
- **International roaming was turned OFF**, and since you're in France, that would block your data — which picture messages need. I've now **enabled roaming** on your line, at no cost. ✓
- You've used 8.7 GB of your 15 GB data allowance for this cycle (cycle ends Feb 28), so you haven't hit your limit. ✓

Now let's check a few settings on the phone itself. MMS (picture messaging) is fussy and needs several things to be right.

Could you please open your phone's **Settings** and tell me what you see at the very top of the screen (the status bar)? I'm looking for things like Airplane Mode, signal bars, "5G" or "4G", and whether mobile data shows as on. If it's easier, just read me everything you see up there.
turns.execution_output: User: Let me look... I'll check that for you now.

turns.thought:
Good news first: **nothing we're about to do touches your photos.** Your pictures live in your phone's storage, not out in the network — changing these settings won't delete anything, and the unsent message will just sit quietly in your messaging app until it goes through. So no need to worry on that score.

And your instinct about "2G" was a good one — yes, 2G is the oldest, slowest kind of connection. It's enough for plain calls and simple texts, but picture messages need a faster connection (3G, 4G, or 5G). Combined with your one bar of signal, that's very likely why the photo is stuck.

Here's what I'd like you to try:

1. Open **Settings**, then tap **Connections** (on some phones it's called **Network & internet**), then **Mobile networks**.
2. Tap **Network mode** (it may be called "Preferred network mode").
3. Choose the option that includes 4G or 5G — something like **"5G/4G/3G auto"** or **"4G/3G/2G auto connect"**. Avoid any option that says 2G only.
4. While you're on that same **Mobile networks** screen, please make sure **Data roaming** is switched **ON**. (I've already turned roaming on for your line on our side; this is the matching switch on the phone itself, and you need both.)
5. Give it about 30 seconds, then look at the top of the screen again and tell me what it says now — I'm hoping to see 4G or 5G instead of 2G.

The exact wording varies a bit between phones, so if a menu doesn't look quite like what I described, tell me what you see and we'll find the right one together. And if we can't get this sorted, I'll get you over to a colleague who can walk through it with you directly.
turns.execution_output: User: Okay, I'll try. Let me see... Settings, then Connections... I think I found Mobile networks. Now Network mode... I see a list. I'm going to pick the one with 4G and 5G.

turns.thought:
Yes — that all sounds right, and it's a big improvement on what you saw before: excellent 5G with data on and roaming on is exactly what we want. You've gone from 2G/one bar to a strong fast connection, so the network side is now in good shape.

Do go ahead and try sending the photo again — it's safe to, and if it goes through, we're done.

One thing worth knowing: picture messages use a separate "gateway" setting from regular data called the **MMSC**. Regular internet can work fine while that gateway address is missing or wrong, which leaves photos stuck even on a perfect 5G connection. So if the message fails again, that's the next thing we'll check.

If it doesn't send, please try this:

1. Open **Settings**, then **Connections** → **Mobile networks** → **Access Point Names** (often shortened to **APN**).
2. You should see your carrier's name with a dot or filled circle next to it. Look for a long list of settings, and find the one called **MMSC** (or "MMS center"). If that field is **empty** or looks garbled, tap the three-dot menu (or "More") and choose **Reset to default**.
3. If you do reset it, please then **restart your phone** completely — hold the power button and choose Restart. This step matters; the change usually won't take effect until the phone restarts.
4. Once it's back on, wait for the signal icon to reappear, then try the photo again.

After that, if it's *still* stuck, we'll look at two last spots: the messaging app's permissions, and a setting called **Wi-Fi Calling** that can sometimes interfere with picture messages.

Take your time — your photo is safe, and restarting your phone won't erase it. Let me know how you get on.
turns.execution_output: User: Let me try sending the photo to my daughter now...

turns.thought:
Yes — tap **Access Point Names**. That's exactly the right place, and I'm sorry it's taken a few steps to get here. You've actually made solid progress: we've ruled out the signal and the roaming, which were real problems. What's left is this gateway setting, which is a very common culprit for picture messages specifically — regular internet can work perfectly while photos still fail. So this is a likely fix, not a shot in the dark.

Once you're in there:

1. You should see your carrier's name listed, probably with a dot or circle marked next to it. **Tap on that name** (not the checkbox) to open its details.
2. Scroll down that list carefully — there's quite a bit in there. Look for **MMSC** (your phone might call it "MMS center" or "Message center").
3. Tell me what's in that field. Roughly, it should look a bit like a web address — letters, dots, and a forward slash or two. **If it's completely empty, or if it looks like nonsense/random characters, that's our problem.**

If it does look wrong or empty:
- Tap the **three-dot menu** in the top corner (or a "More" button), then choose **Reset to default**. Your phone will put the correct carrier settings back.
- Then — and this is the important bit — **restart your phone completely.** Hold the power button, choose Restart. Without the restart the change often doesn't take effect.
- After it comes back on, wait for the signal icon to reappear at the top, then try sending the photo to your daughter again.

Take your time scrolling; that list can be long, and it's easy to miss the MMSC line. And don't worry — resetting the APN to default changes how your phone connects to the network, but it doesn't touch your photos, messages, or contacts.

Let me know what you find in that MMSC field, or just tell me how it goes after the restart if it looked empty.
turns.execution_output: User: Alright, I'm tapping on Access Point Names now. Let me see what's in there...

turns.thought:
I'm sorry this is dragging on — I know it's frustrating when each fix doesn't quite do it. But that's genuinely useful information, so thank you for reading it out to me.

That MMSC value — `http://mms.carrier.com/mms/wapenc` — looks like a properly formed gateway address to me. It's not empty and it's not garbled junk, which is the main thing I was worried about. So I don't think we need to reset the APN after all. Let's leave that alone.

Next thing to try, and this one is a known troublemaker especially when you're abroad:

**Wi‑Fi Calling.** You mentioned Wi‑Fi itself is off, but Wi‑Fi Calling is a separate setting that can stay switched on, and it can sometimes get in the way of picture messages when you're roaming on a foreign network.

1. Go back to **Settings**, then **Connections**.
2. Look for **Wi‑Fi Calling** — on some phones you may need to tap **More connection settings** first. (If you'd rather, just use the search box at the top of Settings and type "Wi‑Fi Calling" — that's often quicker.)
3. If the switch is **on**, tap it to turn it **OFF**.

Then please do the restart we talked about: hold the **power button**, choose **Restart**, wait for the phone to come back and for the signal icon to reappear at the top, and try sending the photo to your daughter again.

Turning this off won't stop your phone from making calls — you're on 5G with mobile data working, so calls and messages go through the cellular network just fine.

If it still won't send after that, we'll check the messaging app's permissions — it needs access to your photos and to text messages in order to send a picture, and occasionally that gets switched off. And if we get through all of that with no luck, I'll hand you over to a technical specialist who can dig in further with you. Either way, we're not giving up on it.
turns.execution_output: User: Okay, let me look for Wi-Fi Calling. I'll use that search box you mentioned...

turns.thought:
You're right again — that's not it either. Wi‑Fi Calling being off is actually the good outcome here, so nothing to change there.

And yes, I'd still like you to restart. I understand the nerves, so let me be very clear and specific about it:

**Your photos are safe.** A restart is just the phone switching off and on again. It doesn't delete anything — not your photos, not your messages, not your contacts. The photo of your grandson is stored on your phone itself, and the unsent message will still be sitting in your messaging app with its little spinning circle when you come back. The only thing a restart does is let the network settings we've changed (roaming, the 5G connection) settle in properly. Think of it like rebooting a laptop when it's being sluggish.

You also have two things in your favour: the photo is still on your phone regardless, and you can always just pick it again from your gallery even if something odd happened to that message.

A couple of practical pointers before you do it:
- Make sure your phone has a bit of charge left, or pop it on the charger first — there's no point adding a flat battery to your day.
- Hold the **power button** until the menu appears, then tap **Restart** (or "Restart"/"Reboot"). If it offers "Power off" instead, that's fine — use that, wait about 20 seconds, then hold the power button again to switch it back on.
- After it comes back on, wait for the signal bars and "5G" to reappear at the top before trying anything. Give it about a minute. Maybe unlock it and let it settle a moment.

Then try sending the photo to your daughter again.

Go ahead and do that now, and let me know what happens. If it still won't go after the restart, the next thing I'd like to check is the messaging app's permissions — whether it's allowed to reach your photos and your texts, since without those it can't attach or send a picture. That's a quick check and an easy fix if that's the cause.

And I'll say again: if we work through that and you're still stuck, I'll pass you to a technical specialist who can take it further. We'll get your grandson's photo to your daughter.
turns.execution_output: User: Alright... I'll do it. My battery's at 80%, so that should be fine. Restarting now.

turns.thought:
I'm sorry, John — I know this has been a long road, and I don't blame you for being frustrated. You've done everything right on your end: strong 5G, roaming on, APN and gateway address fine, Wi‑Fi Calling off, and now a full restart. That's genuinely helped us rule things out, even if it doesn't feel that way.

You're right, permissions are the sensible next thing to check. When a messaging app can't reach your photos or your text messages, it will often look exactly like what you're seeing — the message spins and fails, with no real explanation.

Here's how to check:

1. Open **Settings**, then tap **Apps** (it might be called "Applications" or "App management").
2. You'll get a list of everything on your phone — scroll to your **Messages** app (it may be called "Messages", "Messaging", or "SMS"). Tap it.
3. Tap **Permissions**.
4. You'll now see a list of things the app can or can't use. Look for these two specifically:
   - **Photos and videos** (or "Storage" on older phones) — this is what lets it attach your grandson's photo.
   - **SMS** — this is what lets it send text and picture messages at all.
5. Tell me what it says next to each one. Good would be **"Allow"** or **"Allowed"**. A problem would be **"Denied"**, **"Don't allow"**, or **"Ask every time"**.

If either of those two is not set to Allow:
- Tap on it and choose **Allow** (or "Allow all the time").
- Then try sending the photo again — you shouldn't even need a restart for this one.

If both already say Allow, don't change anything. Instead, on that same app's screen, look for **Mobile data** or **Data usage** and tell me whether **"Allow background data usage"** is on, and whether anything mentions **Data Saver** — background data being switched off would also make a message hang like that.

Take it slowly, and just read out whatever you see — there's no wrong answer, and we'll decide the next step from there. If permissions turn out to be fine too, I'll pass you straight to a technical specialist so you're not stuck going in circles with me.
turns.execution_output: User: Okay, let me find the Messages app... Settings, then Apps... I see "Messages" in the list. Tapping on it, then Permissions.

turns.thought:
Good question, and yes — the naming is confusing because every phone words it differently. "Storage" is almost certainly the same thing as the "photos" permission I mentioned, so that one is fine and it's the important one for attaching the picture.

The **SMS** one does matter — it's what lets the app actually send rather than just attach. But don't panic about not seeing it:

- Scroll **further down** that same permissions list. It's often below the main ones, sometimes under a heading like **"Additional permissions"** or **"Not allowed"**.
- It may be named **"SMS"**, **"Text messages"**, **"Send and view SMS"**, or **"Messages"** — depending on your phone.

Quick way to tell whether it's actually a problem: **are your plain text messages (no photo) sending OK?** If normal texts go through fine, then the SMS permission is working in practice and we can stop worrying about it. If those fail too, that's a strong sign this is the culprit, and tapping it to set it to **Allow** should fix both.

While you're in that app's settings, one more thing to check, and this one fits your symptom well:

- Look for **Mobile data** or **Data usage** on that same screen.
- Check whether **"Allow background data usage"** is ON, and whether anything says **Data Saver**. If either is restricted, the messaging app can be blocked from sending even though your browser works fine — it would spin and fail exactly like you described.

If you can find the SMS entry, tap it and choose **Allow** (or "Allow all the time"), then try the photo again without needing another restart.

If, after sorting those, it's still refusing, the last thing I'd want to rule out is a **VPN**, if you've ever installed one — those can quietly block picture messages while leaving everything else looking normal. Tell me if you recognise that or not, and we'll go from there.

And to be straight with you, John: if we get through permissions, background data and VPN with no luck, I'll put you through to a technical specialist rather than keep sending you round the menus. You've been very patient and you deserve a resolution.
turns.execution_output:
User: Let me check a couple of things. First, plain texts — yes, those do go through fine. Just the pictures don't work.

Let me look at the data usage for the messaging app...
